title: The first enterprise buyer
metaTitle: Pages for a first enterprise buyer
excerpt: Answer the questions a security or procurement reader will ask, on their own page. Keep the homepage about the product, and only write what is true.

faqs.question: Where should enterprise security answers live?
faqs.answer: Put them on a stable page linked from the footer, with the real questions as headings. Keep the homepage about the product. A single text link is enough of a signpost. Do not open the hero with a policy.

faqs.question: What if you have not completed a formal security audit?
faqs.answer: Say so, and say what you do today: where data lives, who can access it, how a customer leaves, and whether you train on their content. A plain statement that you have not finished an audit is safer than a badge you have not earned. Offer a way to ask the person who actually knows.

faqs.question: What should a procurement FAQ contain?
faqs.answer: It should be a visible list of questions and answers on a URL you can forward. Schema.org describes an FAQ page as that kind of page. The markup can wait until the questions are really on the page. The reviewer needs the text.

markdown:
A website for enterprise buyers has two readers. The first is the person who wants the product. The second is the security, legal, or procurement person they must convince. The page should answer the second reader's questions without turning the homepage into a compliance document. The homepage stays an explanation of the product. The answers live one step away, in plain language, and only where you can say them honestly.

You do not need a fake trust center full of badges you have not earned. You need a short, true path for the questions that will arrive the moment a larger company is interested.

## The second reader

The champion inside the buyer already understands the pitch, or they would not be forwarding you. The second reader opens the link cold, often from a mail that says "can we use this?" They look for risk. They will not be persuaded by a hero animation. They will be persuaded by finding the policy, the data answer, and the limit without a scavenger hunt.

Assume they have a checklist, even if you never see it. Where is the data stored. Who can access it. What happens when we leave. Do you use our data to train anything. Who is the company behind the product. Those questions repeat. You can write them once.

Do not make the champion translate you. If they have to write a paragraph in Slack explaining what you told them on a call, that paragraph will be slightly wrong, and the wrongness will become the objection. Put the accurate paragraph on a page they can forward. The champion's job is to point, not to reconstruct.

The second reader is also busy. A 40-page PDF that arrives as "see attached" will be skimmed for the one line they need, or ignored. A page with the questions in text, scannable, will be used. [Schema.org describes FAQPage](https://schema.org/FAQPage) as a page that presents questions and answers. The useful part for you is not the markup first. It is the visible list: real questions, real answers, on a URL that does not change. Markup can follow when the questions are actually on the page. Empty markup over a marketing homepage does nothing for procurement.

## Questions they ask

Start with the set you have already been asked, or the set you know is coming. Write answers you can keep true.

- Who operates the product, and where is the company.
- What data you store, for what purpose, and where it lives.
- Who at your company can access customer data, and why.
- Whether you sell data or use customer content to train a model. The honest yes or no.
- How a customer exports or deletes their data when they leave.
- How long you keep it.
- What you have actually done on security: a named practice, a named provider, a report you can share under NDA, or the plain statement that you have not yet completed a formal audit.
- Accessibility: which standard you aim at, and what you have not finished.

The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the right thing to point to when they ask about accessibility. Say whether you are working toward WCAG, and at what level if you truly are. Do not stamp a conformance badge you have not tested. A short, accurate status beats a logo. If you have a known gap, a procurement reader would rather see the gap than discover it in a pilot.

Leave answers blank in the draft until a person who knows can fill them. A founder guessing at a retention period will create a policy by accident. Policies are promises. Write them with the same care you use for a contract, because they will be pasted into one.

If a question does not apply, say it does not apply, and why. "We do not train models on customer content" is a complete answer when it is true. Silence reads as the answer they fear.

## Where the answers live

Give them a stable URL, linked from the footer and from any security line on the homepage. One page is enough at the start. Call it what it is: security and procurement, or data and access. "Trust" is fine if the page earns the word. It is a poor title for a page of hopes.

On that page, use the questions as headings. The answer follows in a few sentences. Link to a longer PDF only when the PDF exists and is the real document, such as a data processing addendum you are willing to sign. Do not link to a PDF that is a brochure.

Keep the homepage link in the footer, not in the hero. The champion needs the product. The second reader knows how to find a footer. If your early traffic is mostly the second reader, you can add one text link under the main call to action: "Security and data." That is a signpost, not a second homepage.

When a questionnaire arrives, answer it from this page, and when the questionnaire asks something new that you can answer publicly, add it to the page. The page becomes the memory. The next questionnaire gets faster. The next founder-to-seller handoff gets calmer. This is the same habit as keeping brand files and docs in one place after a project, the way a client portal should. Scattered answers in old emails will contradict each other.

Date the page when the substance changes. Do not bump the date on a schedule to look active. A procurement reader compares versions. A fake freshness is obvious and it costs the credibility the page exists to build.

## The homepage stays a homepage

The homepage still says who the product is for and what they do with it. It does not list your subprocessors in the hero. It does not open with a paragraph about encryption. Those facts matter to the second reader and bore or alarm the first if they are the only story.

One line is enough on the homepage if you want a signal: "Security and data practices are documented here." The word here is the link. The product story continues. A buyer who cares will click. A buyer who does not will not be dragged through a policy.

Pricing for a larger company can be "talk to us" only if that is the real motion. If you have a floor, you can say the floor. Enterprise buyers do not need a three-tier grid with a cartoon rocket. They need to know whether a conversation is plausible. A sentence does that.

Proof stays true. A logo of a large company you have not sold to is a direct way to fail the second reader, because they may work there, or know someone who does. Named work you can discuss, or no logo. The absence will not kill a first conversation. A false logo might.

## What you can say before the audit

You can say what you do. You store data in a named provider and region. You restrict access to named roles. You encrypt in transit. You have backups, and you have tested a restore, or you have not. You will sign a reasonable addendum, or you will not yet. Each of these is a sentence, and each must be accurate on the day a lawyer reads it.

You can say what you have not done. "We have not completed SOC 2" is a legitimate sentence for an early company. Many first enterprise conversations survive it if the rest of the answers are plain and the product is worth the process. The conversation dies faster on a badge that does not exist. Do not borrow a vendor's certification and imply it is yours. You may say the vendor has it, if that is true and relevant, and you should still describe your own layer.

Offer a call with the person who actually knows. For a while that person is the founder or the engineer who runs the system. Put a path on the security page for "questions this page does not answer." The second reader would rather have a precise mail than a chat widget staffed by someone reading a script.

Update the page when the truth changes. An old "we do not store files" line, left up after you started storing files, is the kind of inconsistency that ends a review. Put a reminder in the same checklist as a release. If the release changes data, the page changes in the same week.

## What to add when the first one arrives

When the first serious buyer appears, resist a new brand and a new site. Add the page if it does not exist. Fill the answers they asked. Send the URL in the thread, and use the thread to correct any answer that was vague. Then stop. Do not spend the month building a compliance microsite while the champion is waiting for a data addendum.

Prepare the addendum, the list of subprocessors, and the export answer as documents you can attach. Keep them identical to the page. If the attachment and the page disagree, the reviewer will choose the worse reading.

After you have done this once, you will know which questions were theater and which were real. Keep the real ones. The next buyer will ask them too. The homepage can remain a product page the whole time. That is the point. The company looks larger because it is clear, not because it published a binder.

Partners will show up next, and someone will ask for a logo wall. A wall does not explain what the partnership does for the customer. The page that does is the next one to write: [a partner page that is not a logo dump](/blog/a-partner-page-that-is-not-a-logo-dump).
